extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalism students, and practicing journalists interested in investigative/reporting methods
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for producing investigative journalism — long-form, deeply researched reporting that uncovers hidden problems, corruption, abuse of power, and other matters of public interest. Covers defining features, methods/tools, ethics, collaboration, funding, and historical examples of impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core definition / focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative journalism is a genre of journalism in which reporters deeply investigate a single or few topics of interest, such as hidden problems and truths, serious crimes, education, racial injustice, corruption and abuse of power, social welfare, and corporate wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes depth on a limited set of topics rather than routine beat reporting; subjects are often matters of significant public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and resource investment
rubrics_metrics.description: An investigative journalist may spend months or years researching and preparing a report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations are often time-consuming and expensive; reporters and organizations should plan for long lead times and allocate sufficient resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watchdog / accountability mission
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners sometimes use the terms 'watchdog reporting' or 'accountability reporting' — investigative journalism seeks to discover the truth and identify lapses, holding power to account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports are often intended to prompt public awareness, reform, legal action, or institutional change; framing and evidence should support accountability aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from legal/regulatory investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative journalism is distinct from work done by police, lawyers, auditors, and regulatory bodies in that it is not limited as to target, not legally founded and is closely connected to publicity (per Hugo de Burgh).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists operate independently of legal mandates; they should understand but not conflate journalistic investigation with official investigatory powers and constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document analysis (lawsuits, tax records, filings, reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use analysis of documents, such as lawsuits and other legal documents, tax records, government reports, regulatory reports, and corporate financial filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful examination of primary documents is central; documentation provides verifiable evidence and should be cross-checked and cited where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public records and databases
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searching and combining public-record databases helps reveal patterns and connections; maintain records of queries and provenance for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical investigation / scrutiny of practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigation of technical issues, including scrutiny of government and business practices and their effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May require subject-matter expertise or consultation with experts to interpret technical materials and assess systemic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research into social and legal issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Research into social and legal issues is part of investigative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual research situates findings within broader social, legal, and policy frameworks to show significance and implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription research services (e.g., LexisNexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of subscription research sources such as LexisNexis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paid databases provide access to archival materials, court records, and specialized reporting tools; account for cost in project planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews: on-the-record and anonymous sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous interviews with on-the-record sources as well as, in some instances, interviews with anonymous sources (for example whistleblowers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corroborate anonymous-sourced claims with documents or other testimony; protect source identity when necessary and follow ethical/legal protocols for handling whistleblowers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of Information requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of federal or state Freedom of Information Acts to obtain documents and data from government agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FOI requests are a key means to obtain official records; practitioners must understand procedures, exemptions, appeal processes, and likely timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSINT (open-source intelligence) tools
rubrics_metrics.description: OSINT databases and tools that contain free and open resources that anybody can use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage publicly available digital sources (social media, registries, satellite imagery, leaked datasets) while validating provenance and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-assisted / database journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of computer-assisted reporting or database journalism (example: Bill Dedman's 'The Color of Money' as an early example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data analysis, cleaning, and visualization can reveal systemic patterns; teams should include data skills or collaborate with data journalists/statisticians and document methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undercover investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Undercover investigation (example: Nellie Bly feigned insanity to investigate a lunatic asylum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undercover work can uncover concealed practices but raises significant ethical and legal concerns; use only when public interest cannot be served by other means and after editorial/legal review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration and international teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations are increasingly carried out by news organizations working together, even internationally (e.g., Panama Papers, Paradise Papers, ICIJ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-organizational collaboration pools resources and expertise for large, complex investigations; coordinate standards for data sharing, verification, legal risk, and publication timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding and sustainability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative journalism has become harder to fund due to declines in advertising revenue; nonprofit and worker-owned models have been used to support investigative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project planning should consider funding sources (grants, nonprofit support, public donations), budget realistic timelines, and the financial sustainability of investigation units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics, legal risk, and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical and safety considerations including freedom of information, freedom of the press (defamation, safety), and source protection; journalists may face legal or physical threats (example: Hopewell Chin'ono's arrest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize source protection, legal review for defamation risk, personal safety protocols, and organizational policies for high-risk reporting; prepare for potential retaliation or legal challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for demonstrable public impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical examples show investigative journalism can lead to tangible reforms and accountability (e.g., Ida Tarbell on Standard Oil, Upton Sinclair's 'The Jungle' leading to FDA creation, Watergate prompting Nixon's resignation, Spotlight exposing abuse in the Archdiocese of Boston).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reporting to show clear evidence and pathways to impact (policy change, prosecutions, institutional reform), and document outcomes where possible to demonstrate public value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic and professional development
rubrics_metrics.description: There are university departments teaching investigative journalism, and conferences presenting peer-reviewed research into investigative journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should engage with academic research and professional development to stay current on methods, ethics, and tools; peer-reviewed studies can inform best practices.
